title: Practice Period 2 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up lines 9 through 17 of the Sandokai, Shitou's eighth-century poem on the interplay of Ji, the things of the world, and Ri, emptiness or unity. After zazen and a chant of the full text, Nomon looks at how the mind sorts the senses into pleasant and unpleasant, tracing the repeated Chinese character for "interact" to pieces meaning walk and turn around. A Dogen poem about waterbirds that leave no traces leads into a reading from Mingyur Rinpoche's In Love with the World, where the lama, newly vanished from his monastery, is squeezed onto the lowest-class Indian train, sits on the floor for the first time, and catches himself judging the passengers' smell and dirty feet.

sentences.text: Anyway, welcome or welcome back to this little exploration of this Chinese Zen poem, Chan poem, from the eighth century, written by Master Shi Toh, that we think is important, or at least we think it's important because it showed up in our chant book, so it must be important, because that's how religion goes.
I was listening to an interesting interview with a philosopher who studies Buddhism a lot, named Evan Thompson.

He's got a new book out called *Why I'm Not a Buddhist*, and he says one of the reasons he's not a Buddhist is he thinks most of the Western Buddhists are a little confused and think that Buddhism isn't really a religion, so that freaks him out as a philosopher, so he doesn't want to come here.
So I'm sorry to tell you, it's a religion.
Oh wow.
It's a good one, I hope.
What does that mean?

It seems like it makes some kind of sense, but not completely, so that's the problem: there's a little gap between mostly making sense and completely making sense where we can get a little frustrated.
I actually got a little frustrated last week trying to make this poem make sense for you, so I let that go.
We'll enjoy it more if we don't try to make it totally make sense, I think.

I appreciate Master Shurto's effort to loosen us up, because the big theme of the poem is this vast interplay between all the things we can see and think, the stuff of the world, which gets referred to by this character on the left, which is pronounced Ji in Japanese.

Mostly I'm talking about the Chinese pronunciation, but since we're a Japanese lineage, and all the commentaries we're likely to run into are by Japanese priests, and they use the Japanese pronunciations, they talk about Ji, the stuff of the world.
That's where we're hanging out and trying to have a clash.
So it's about the interplay between that and the stuff of the world.
Sort of beyond idea, pointed to by the other character here, upper right, Ri, which points to unity, sameness, emptiness, everything beyond the world of things.
When I'm talking to you and we're talking to each other, when we're reading the text and trying to think about this stuff, we're bound up in the world of language and concepts.
So I thought maybe the smart thing to do, which is what we mostly do around here, is sit in silence.
Let's do a few minutes of meditation, or zazen.
This is a poem that points to what Zen is, and zazen just means sitting Zen.
So let's sit the poem for a few minutes anyway, and then we'll talk.
Sitting is an embodied thing, right?
So finding a posture: upright, balanced, spine nice and long, chest open, breathing.
We can appreciate the sound of the bell, the feeling of our breath and our body.
And then let all that go and just sit.
When we say just sit, that's actually what we're talking about: just sit.
If thoughts appear, maybe we can perceive the thoughts as no different from anything else, no different from sensations in the body or sounds, the temperature on your skin.
Just more stuff in the world of Ji.
Moments in between perceptions, or behind perceptions, or a feeling that's broader or bigger than the sum of our experiences, might be some echo of Ri.
I'm going to ring the bell to close.
Let's see if we can stay with the sound of the bell to where there's no sound of the bell.
It might be another way to explore the things of Ji and the non-things of Ri.
Can we experience the sound and the non-sound of the bell?
Thanks.
The sound is on a long time, huh?
How do we know it's not still going on?
It's just our perception.
Let's tuck you in somewhere.
Okay, great.
No worries, it happens.
I counted 31 rings one time, but this time I counted 26.
**Participant:** What do you mean by rings?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** I mean, after...
**Participant:** Oscillations in the sound wave?
You were counting them?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Let's chant the whole text.
I'll do an introduction with the title and we'll chant it through.
*Converging of difference and unity.
The mind of the great sages in India is intimately transmitted from west to east.
While human faculties are sharp or dull, the way has no northern or southern ancestors.
The spiritual shore shines clear in the light.
The branching streams flow on in the dark.*
*Grasping at things is surely delusion.
According with sameness is still not enlightenment.
All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement.
Otherwise each keeps its place.
Sites vary in quality and form.
Sounds differ as pleasing or harsh.
Refined in a common speech come together in the dark.
Rare and murky phrases are distinguished in the light.
The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire eats, wind moves, water wets.*
*On this solid.
Eye and sights, ear and hearing sounds, nose and smells, tongue and taste.
Thus with each and every thing, depending On these roots the leaves spread forth.
Trunk and branches share the essence of the word.
In common each has its speech.
In the light there is darkness but don't take it as darkness.
Though in the dark there is light but don't see it as light.
Light and dark propose one another like a front and back foot in walking.
Each of the myriad things has its merit, expressed according to function and place.
Phenomena exist, box and lid fit.*
*Principle response, arrow points meet.
Hearing the words understand the meaning.
Don't set up standards of your own.
If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near.
But if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.
In fact we urge you who study the mystery: do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
Thanks.
Just to recap a little from last week for those who aren't here and those who don't remember, or maybe I'll say it a different way this week and I'll make more or less sense.
If you have a pen, you might want to make a line between 8 and 9, because the topic changes every eight lines until the end.
Last week we looked at lines 1 through 8. [unclear: "Suzuki is a book by Suzuki Roshi reading that"].
It's the first three chapters of the book.
And it's an intro.
Most texts...
Where did this come from?
It's important, and we can all make use of it even if we're smart or dull.
So it's talking to the audience too.
It's trying to reassure us.
And in lines 7 and 8 it gives the kernel of the whole text.
Lines 1 through 6 are the setup, and sorry, 5 and 6 are also encouragement, that there's a deep matter at hand.
And 7 and 8 are the main topics.
So if you look carefully at lines 7 and 8: *Grasping at things is surely delusion.

According with sameness is still not enlightenment.* And if you have really good eyes or your readers on, you'll see the second character of line 7 is this character here, which is translated in this translation as "things."
So the stuff of the world.
Grasping the stuff of the world is surely delusion.
Trying to lock it down, trying to make ourselves happy with the stuff of the world, is not going to work out.
The social media feed is endlessly not quite satisfying.
That's what he was thinking about.
Line 7 is a setup for line 8.
And in line 8 the second character is this one here on the right, Ri in Japanese, which means emptiness, unity, interpenetration and all these ideas.

You would think that if you could just chill out into enlightenment, emptiness, going beyond, whatever it is you call it, and wish would happen in zazen, and maybe it does and maybe it doesn't, you would think that would solve the whole deal, and you would be peaceful and happy forever.
But he knocks that straw man down right away.
He says that according with sameness, being in accordance with this Ri, this unity, this harmony, this emptiness, this everythingness, that's not it either.
So this is all to make you interested in reading the rest of the poem.
Like, okay, well, what do we do?
So let's look at the next eight lines.
You might want to put another line between lines 16 and 17.
We're going to look at 9 through 17, the next eight lines.
Now he's bringing it to ground.
We're immersed in this world with our six senses.
In the West we say five senses, right?
That's the physical stuff that we can touch, taste, feel, hear and see.
And in the West we divide all the physical stuff from the mental stuff, and the mind is a whole different thing.
But in Buddhist psychology there are a lot of different words that get translated as mind.
What I'm thinking about here is amanas in Sanskrit, and that means the mind that identifies thoughts.
So that's sense number six.
This is an important point all by itself: maybe there's not really a difference between stuff-stuff and thought-stuff.
Maybe it's just all stuff, all just Ji.
And maybe it does us a disservice to treat thinking as some special category of things.
Maybe that might be another source of suffering.
Another point I was trying to make last week too was that there's some intricate philosophy in here, a lot of which I don't completely understand, to be honest.
But we can always take heart, even if it looks intricate, in remembering that the whole point in a Buddhist text should be freedom from suffering.
Freedom from suffering involves trying to understand something, like why do we suffer?
The root idea in Buddhism is we don't suffer because we're broken exactly, even though we might think that.
We suffer because we don't understand the nature of the world and the nature of ourselves, and we're looking in all the wrong places, scrolling the social media feed for happiness and so on.
But if we understood the nature of things, then suffering would just be a strange memory.
Like, what was that thing?
I used to be like, what was that thing?
Unhappy?
What was that thing?
I can't remember that thing.
So that's the idea of it.
The next part is a dip into the senses.
But just remember that when they say senses, they're not excluding thinking.
*All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement.
Otherwise each keeps its place.
Sites vary in quality and form.
Sounds differ as pleasing or harsh.
Refined and common speech come together in the dark.
Clear and murky phrases are distinguished in the light.*
Let's take some of this a little bit apart.
What was I going to say?
This is about, as we look at the senses, appreciating, within the realm of Ji, which is where we tend to hang out, where we can make sense of things, that there are also two sides of things.
There's always two sides of things.

And the more multidimensional we can be, and the more we can see both sides of everything, the better off we're going to be, and the better situated we'll be to understand this ultimate two-sidedness, which is not one and not two.
That's Ji and Ri.
So it's looking at the way everything on the one hand seems to be separate.
The objects of the senses means everything we can perceive, so that's like the universe, right?
The other thing about Buddhist psychology: we have the idea of an external reality that I'm over here perceiving, and in Buddhist psychology it's flipped the other way too.
There's only the perception.
Who knows about the external reality?
When we compare notes, it sounds like it's probably similar, but it's completely unknowable.
And this shows up in the West too, right?
This is like the allegory of Plato's cave.
Who knows what's really out there, but we're all seeing some similar shadow play.
So the objects of the senses means everything.
So everything interacts and yet it doesn't.
Things seem to be different and yet we know they're all interacting, and we can see it from either point of view.
They can be stable, they can be in motion, but ultimately it's both, right?
It's always both.
That's the first half of the four: *The objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement.
Otherwise each keeps its place.*
Then it goes on to talk about another division that we do.
It's talking next about the way the mind so rapidly and strongly divides everything up also into pleasant and unpleasant, into stuff we like and stuff we don't like.
This is the second skandha of early Buddhism, the mental factor of vedana, of feeling tone, or feelings.
When we chant the Heart Sutra, it's in there: no form, no feelings, no perceptions.
Does that sound familiar?
Feelings there is the translation of this.
And it's not feelings like emotions.
It's this feeling tone of things: like it, don't like it.
So pleasing or harsh, refined or common, clear or murky.
As we use the world that we are in, the world of things, we can start to get more refined about the way that we're making it into the universe that we're perceiving.
So it's not this neutral external universe.
It's a construction that we're constructing.
This section is talking about the construction of the universe by us.
We're seeing interaction, we're seeing stability, we're seeing pleasing stuff, we're seeing harsh stuff, we're seeing stuff we like, we're seeing stuff we don't like.
I want to go back for a minute just to lines 10 and 11.
Here it would be helpful to flip to the more detailed breakdown, where I went nuts with the Chinese dictionary.
We wasted way too much time, but now it's done.
So let's find, I didn't put the numbers on the verse numbers, so I wish I had.
Yeah, let's find "interact and yet do not."
Which page is that on?
Is that on the second page?
Second page, second page.
Okay, "interact and yet do not."
Yeah, at the bottom of the second page: interacting and yet do not, and then interacting brings involvement.
I was interested in this question of what we are talking about, like interacting.
Why does it keep repeating that?
So I went to the characters there, and I noticed that in those two lines the same character shows up three times.
It's pronounced h-u-i, something like hui.
I had the online pronouncing guide tell me that.
It's a rising tone, hui.
And that's this character here, hui.
I don't know, just for fun, I looked up the pieces of that.
It's a compound character with a left side and a right side.
In Chinese etymology, usually there are additional hints to a meaning, or at least Dharma teachers say there are, maybe just so they can fill up time in the lecture.
That's an ancient tradition, so I might as well make use of it.
This character, hui, as a whole, here I wrote "return" or "turn," and I looked it up some more, and the character as a whole also means revolving, rotating, curving, or zigzagging.
So very dynamic, you know?
The reality of interaction here is very dynamic.
Things are really in motion.
And then this part on the left side, which by itself is pronounced cho, a falling tone, cho, in Chinese means walking.
So there's something in here about walking on the left half of this character that means turning, revolving, curving, returning.
And then the little box inside a box, which is really fun to brush, actually, that is also, for some reason, called hui, the same as the big overall thing, and it means to turn around.
This character that repeats three times, all about the dynamic nature of reality, and that gets translated in English, in this case, as interaction, seems to break down as walk and turn around.
I thought, well, that's interesting.
Maybe a journey is implied here, that we have to walk around.
We have to walk out into our lives and we're going to get turned around.
It's not going to be a straight path, right?
It makes me think also of the wonderful Western trope, which shows up in Asia too, of the hero's journey, like Odysseus.
You've got to take a great journey out to learn what you need to learn, you eventually have to get home somehow, but you return home transformed.
So there's a process here in understanding reality, and a process implies not just thinking about stuff, right?
A process implies practice.

So this is my supposition, that this character, about interaction, about returning, about walking and turning around, implies that we need to practice with reality, and not just practice with emptiness, but practice with things.
Practice with the senses.
Enter the world through what we do actually perceive and get really curious about its nature.

If we actually just try to check out, and somehow set down all the senses, let's go live in the flotation tank, I think it's like $60 an hour, so you can't afford that, with no senses, so you can somehow try to just zoom in, leave Ji behind, leave things behind, and zoom in on Ri, on this universal nature of things, and things beyond things.
That's not going to work out.
You're going to miss something really important.
You're going to miss the things of the world.
And the other reason is that this is a Mahayana Buddhist text, so the other underlying idea here is always that our intention is to be bodhisattvas, to be the beings that go out and help.
So it's good to have monks.
They definitely help, and it's important that we practice and sit here and do nothing.
But we also need to work with the things of the world to help.
Anyway, I thought that was interesting.
So practice is implied, practicing in the world.
And back to these lines about preferences and lines 12 through 15 about sights and sounds and speech and phrases: we need to really study that.
We need to really study the way we divide things up so rapidly, and we justify our division.
We always think, "Oh, I'm absolutely right.
That is bad, and that is good."
Maybe you had opinions like that today about the political moves.
It's possible.
But it's not just big things.
It's everything.
If you watch your mind: I like that, I like that, I don't like that, I like that, I don't like that, I don't like that, no, I don't like that.
I like him, I don't like her.
And part of the problem with that, what we're doing there without really noticing it, which is in opposition to this whole process, is that we're trying to fix things.
When we say, "I don't like Republicans," or "I don't like whatever," I can't think of an example of things you don't like, but maybe there are Republicans here, we do like you.
Whatever you don't like, you're saying this thing has an unlikable quality.
So you're giving it some kind of inherent quality.
And that's what this is saying isn't really happening.
Things have appearances, there's diversity, there's stuff.
When the lights are on, we can see differences.

But actually, the nature of them is also happening in the dark where we can't see, where they're mixing and changing and interacting, and there's no such thing exactly as a Democrat or Republican as a fixed entity.
They're much more fluid than that.
So this has political relevance too, I decided.
Sometimes all this talk doesn't help us, so I'll read you a few poems from Dogen.
I was going to email them and I forgot, so I made a handout of poems.
I think this is almost all of the extant poems by Dogen translated into English, but I don't know if I made enough.
I don't remember how many I printed out.
So I'll just pass that out, and then we can appreciate a poem or two as a way to point to this.
And then I've got a little reading for you that hopefully will point to this in some other way, and then we'll have some dialogue.
Did I make enough of those?
Oh, no, I didn't.
I'll bring more next week and I will email it.
But let me just share a couple.
I can't remember now which ones I shared last week.
What I was really struck by this week is that even though we're in the world of things, all of us from time to time have powerful, beyond-thing experiences with things.
Even though we really only have language and the senses and our mind, somehow, sometimes things are different than things.
I think we can all think about it, and remember, if we think about it for a little while, moments where things were just somehow such.
For me it's often in nature.
Maybe it is for you, but it can be any time.
Sometimes a bird flies by, and you just say, "Oh, whatever."
A seagull.
Other times a bird flies by, and you go, "Ah."
Is the bird somehow better or worse, or are you better or worse, or is something just lining up, when you're not only in the world of G, but feeling into the world of Ri?
So I think of this poem on the left column here, second from the bottom, by Dogen.
*Waterbirds going and coming, their traces disappear, but they never forget their path.*
*Waterbirds going and coming, their traces disappear, but they never forget their path.*
So some bird just flies across the sky.
No trace.
How did that happen?
And yeah, you can go back to the world of G: "Oh, I know, it happens.
The wing is this, and the feathers, and they evolved from dinosaurs, and the habitat must still be okay, thank goodness."
But that's not it, really.
I mean, that is it, but that's not it.
There's something beyond yet.

So what I suggested as a very open-ended homework, I hope it made some kind of sense, was really to open up to that this last week, and I'll be curious in a minute to hear what you noticed about the genus of things.
First let me share a little reading with you.
Hopefully we'll make this all clear and murky at the same time.
I've been appreciating a lot a book lately by a Tibetan named Mingyur Rinpoche called In Love with the World.
It's a really interesting book.
Maybe you heard about this guy.
He was a prominent Tibetan lama, not that old, in his early 30s when this happened, who one day just vanished on purpose.
He had trained in Tibetan Buddhism from a young age, because he's a reincarnated tolku, so they start training at three or four years old or something like that.
And he wasn't exactly just sitting on his butt.

He was in monastic education very intensively, with lots of meditation, and this particular guy was actually the subject of some meditation studies with brain scanners and stuff, and he's just off the charts in every dimension.
He's done an unbelievable number of hours of meditation, 50 or 60,000 hours or something, one of the world-class meditators.
He did two three-year retreats in his teens, just insane.
But in his early 30s he felt like, even though I'm this Buddhist meditation master and everything, I'm stuck in this world of things.
Everywhere I go, I have assistants, and everybody who comes to see me loves me and praises me, and I have special seats, and I've never bought a train ticket on my own.
I hardly even know how money works.
And I'm a little bit like the stories of the Buddha.
I'm in my palace here in the monastery.
He's the abbot of the monastery.
Everywhere he goes, people are helping him.
So he decided he needed to go out into the world and see what it would be like to just practice in the ordinary world, and practice as a beggar, to be truly homeless.
That's in the language of Buddhism: the monks are the ones who leave home.
So in a way he did.
He wasn't living in his nuclear family, because he was this tolku.
But he was in this home, this monastery, kind of pampered.
So he leaves a note.
He actually snitches money from the donations for a while.
It's kind of great, all the precepts that we take.
And he saves a hundred bucks.
And he leaves a note and vanishes in the middle of the night, hops in a taxi, goes to the train station.
Now he's getting on the train to Varanasi in India in this section.
He weaves together the story of this with teachings about Buddhism, which amounts to this stuff, form and emptiness.
Here I am, this high Tibetan lama, but on the other hand I'm like a baby in the world.
So how will my practice show up here?
He's getting on the train, but usually he would get on a night train.
There are three or four classes on the train.
I haven't been on Indian trains, but I've read about them.
Anyone here been on Indian trains?
A couple of us have.
So he's getting on the lowest class train, because his hundred dollars has got to last quite a long time, open-ended.
He doesn't even know when he's going to come back, if ever.
Imagine that.
So here are a few pages from Mingyur Rinpoche, and hopefully you'll appreciate this in terms of interacting with things.
The other underlying idea here is that our identity gets to be based on this too.
That's really the deeper point.
If our identity is just things, then that's also unreliable, unsubstantial, not satisfying.
We're going to suffer because of our identity.
So he has an identity too: important Tibetan lama, Mingyur Rinpoche.
All right, so here's what he wrote.

*When the train pulled in, passengers grabbed their children, their animals, their big suitcases, their enormous cloth sacks tied with rope and strapped around their foreheads and pushed and shoved to get into the car.
My backpack kept getting snagged and I had to lurch forward to disengage it.
I was the last one in and began the train ride in terror.
Squashed flat against the door, my head, torso, and legs pressed between the door and human bodies.
I could see nothing, but took note of the awful smell.
I had to open my mouth and suck in whatever air was available.*
*For the next several minutes, I could not keep my mind from feeling overwhelmed.
My training had introduced me to the spacious awareness of my natural mind.*
So that's a little bit like ri.
*We compare this awareness to open skies and oceans, references meant to invoke immeasurable vastness, even though awareness is more immeasurable than skies and oceans combined and can ever be.

And once we learn to recognize the ever-present quality of awareness, to let go of the conditioned and contingent mind, and recognize that we are this spacious awareness, then our thoughts and emotions manifest as waves or clouds inseparable from awareness.
With recognition of this, we no longer get carried away by the stories that keep our minds spinning in repetitive cycles or jumping around like a crazy monkey.
If we keep our minds entangled with these stories, then it's hard to recognize awareness.
The weather systems within awareness, as we all know, often become quite stormy.
But the more familiar we are with awareness as an innate quality of mind, the less effect the weather has on us.
Waves arise, clouds move by.
When we're not stuck inside them, they lose their impact.
Our sensitivity deepens, and we learn to trust the knowingness of the aware mind.*
*I have known waves of hurricane strength in my life, but not for a very long time.
But now, on this jam-packed train, I was not quite sure if my constricted breath came from the pressure on my face or the fear in my heart.
After a few minutes, the strong energy of fear began to subside.
My breathing slowed.
At the same time, spacious awareness presented itself as if to meet the wave.
Sometimes this happens.
It's as if the force of the turbulence itself allows awareness to be recognized more easily than at other times, and big emotion leads to the big sky-like mind.
I was no longer swept away by the wave and no longer felt like I was drowning.
What I had to do was let it be.
There was no point trying to run away.
The wave was there, though I would have preferred to be somewhere else.
I could now just acknowledge that and stay with the situation, the spacious awareness, and the unpleasant sensation.
When we stay with a reality vaster than the skies, the destructive impact of our wild and disturbed reactions automatically diminishes.
Both clouds or waves don't disappear.
They dissolve and arise again.*
*With each stop of the train, people pushed their way off.
More people boarded.
I went farther forward until I was able to take a spot on the floor and sat cross-legged with my pack in my lap.
Another entirely new experience.
Within Tibetan culture, reincarnated adepts like myself take higher seats than others and it's taboo for tokus to sit on the floor.*
So he had literally never sat on the floor before.
*Seeing me like this would have distressed Tibetan people, but no one here cared about me or my status.
And anyway, to stick to my intentions, I would have to shed a lot of local customs.
I was not habituated to first class, but I was keenly aware of my discomfort with this utterly new environment.
The walls and benches were a kind of putrid green, and in the dingy light, everything looked like it was growing mold.
I arranged this, I reminded myself.
I decided to be here, I said to myself, to travel with people who are deemed unimportant in the world and who are not valued by society.
So who is experiencing this discomfort?
The esteemed Rinpoche?
The privileged abbot?
Or the fixed mind that holds these titles in place?
But my eyes were not in neutral gear.
They were not just seeing sights and not just resting on objects.
Instead, the figures around me were becoming alien creatures, others, those, those over there.
Their dirty clothes obscured my heart.
I was faulting their cracked bare feet, yet soon my own would look just as filthy.

Their body odor was repellent, even though the humidity and the heat and the absence of air conditioning must have left my body smelling just as bad, for the shirt under my robe was glued to my torso with sweat.
Once again, my body was in one place, and my mind was in another.
One was wrapped in the monk's persona, but my experiences were shaped by judgments of the most ordinary kind.
It was like a waking dream.
The dream had the strangeness of an environment that is familiar but somehow totally different.
Or maybe it was me who was different.
I was out of place.
I was out of place in this new world.
It was almost as if I'd walked into someone else's dream.
And this dream did not want me in it as much as I did not want to be in this dream, but here I was.
And it was my dream after all.
And it was the dream I had chosen.
I don't have to like this dream.
Just let it be.
Don't get stuck in it.
Just let it take care of itself.
I did not feel any connection to these people.
Despite years of practices that are supposed to activate spontaneous compassion, I had to reach back in memory for basic reminders.
Everyone wants happiness.
No one wants suffering.
They too have known joy and distress just like me.
They too have lost loved ones.
They too have known fear and kindness.
They too will die just as I will.
For a few minutes I repeated these reminders with genuine sincerity.
Then aversion resurfaced.
Until this night I had imagined my retreat landscape in terms of caves and pristine mountain lakes and village lanes.
And then I remembered a friend who rode the lowest class trains like these.
He had described the rides as very pleasant.
The benches are hard and sometimes the cars are crowded but the windows stay open.
Fresh air comes in and you can buy tea at every stop.
That had sounded fine to me.
But I had never imagined anything like this.
For the next few hours I was both teacher and student reviewing lessons as if I were back in the monastery kindergarten.
Where does this aversion come from?
How does it arise?
My body?
From the outside world?
My breathing was shallow.
I intentionally tried to slow and deepen my breath.
My mind continued to question and comment and judge every little detail.
Noticing this I understood that I had to turn my attention to the judging mind itself.
Are my reactions true?
Are my assumptions correct?
Where do they come from?
